issue.issue_text: Regarding the conduct of the trial for an offence under Section 409, Penal Code, 1860, and which court has the competent jurisdiction to try the case.

facts: The appellant was being tried for an offense under Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), among other offenses.
The punishment for an offense under Section 409 IPC is imprisonment for life or for a term up to 10 years, plus a fine.
The trial was being conducted in the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM).
Under Section 29 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.PC), a CJM is not competent to impose a sentence of imprisonment for more than 7 years.
Both the prosecution and the defense agreed that the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate was not competent to try the offense under Section 409 IPC due to this sentencing limitation.
law: **Section 409, IPC:** Prescribes the punishment for criminal breach of trust by a public servant, banker, etc., as imprisonment for life or up to 10 years.
**First Schedule to Cr.PC:** States that an offense under Section 409 IPC is triable by a Magistrate of the First Class (which includes a CJM).
**Section 29, Cr.PC:** Limits the sentencing power of a Chief Judicial Magistrate to a maximum of 7 years imprisonment.
**Article 21, Constitution of India:** Guarantees the right to a fair trial for both the accused and the prosecution.
application: The Court identified a significant conflict: while the First Schedule of the Cr.PC allows a Magistrate to try a Section 409 IPC case, the Magistrate's sentencing power under Section 29 Cr.PC is insufficient to impose the maximum punishment prescribed by law for that offense.

The Court reasoned that allowing a CJM to try the case would render the statutory punishment of life imprisonment or up to 10 years partially 'otiose' (ineffective), as the court could never impose a sentence beyond 7 years, regardless of the crime's severity.

The Court examined the legislative intent, noting that for most serious offenses punishable with life imprisonment or 10 years, the First Schedule designates the 'Court of Session' as the trial court. It concluded that serious offenses warrant trial by a court with the full power to impose the prescribed sentence.

The Court emphasized that a fair trial requires the case to be heard by a court with competent jurisdiction. A trial before a court that cannot impose the full range of statutory punishment is prejudicial to the prosecution and detrimental to society, as it undermines the object of penology, which is to grant a just and proportionate sentence.

The Court determined that the 'sole solution' to this jurisdictional anomaly is for the trial to be conducted by a Court of Session. A Court of Session has the authority to impose any sentence authorized by law, including life imprisonment, thereby ensuring it has the full competence to try the offense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that to ensure a fair trial and to give full effect to the penal provisions of Section 409 IPC, the trial for this offense must be conducted by a Court of Session, which has the competent jurisdiction to impose the entire range of punishments prescribed. The Court, therefore, ordered the case to be committed from the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate to the appropriate Court of Session for trial.

issue.issue_text: Regarding the exercise of powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure for the committal of a case to the Court of competent jurisdiction, specifically whether the power under Section 323, Cr.PC could be legally exercised.

facts: The appellant was being tried by the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) for several offenses, including one under Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code.
The maximum punishment for an offense under Section 409 IPC is life imprisonment, but the CJM's sentencing power is limited to a maximum of 7 years.
The appellant had already been incarcerated for more than 8 years, which is longer than the maximum sentence the CJM could impose.
The trial was still in its early stages, with only 10 out of 86 prosecution witnesses having been examined.
law: Section 323 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.PC) states that if, during any inquiry or trial, it appears to a Magistrate that the case is one which "ought to be tried by the Court of Session," the Magistrate shall commit it to that Court at any stage before signing the judgment.
The Court clarified that the term "Magistrate" as used in Section 323 includes a "Chief Judicial Magistrate."
application: The Supreme Court determined that the conditions for invoking Section 323 were met in this case.

The Court reasoned that the case "ought to be tried by the Court of Session" because the potential punishment for the offense (life imprisonment) far exceeded the CJM's sentencing authority (7 years).

The "peculiar circumstances" of the case, particularly the fact that the appellant had already been detained for over 8 years (a period longer than the CJM could sentence), made the committal to a competent court necessary and urgent.

The Court found that exercising the power under Section 323 was the proper legal procedure to resolve this issue and ensure the case was tried by a court with the appropriate jurisdiction to impose a fitting sentence if the appellant were convicted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the power under Section 323 of the Cr.PC could be legally exercised. Given the circumstances, it held that this was a case that ought to be tried by the Court of Session and directly ordered the Chief Judicial Magistrate to commit the case to the appropriate Court of Session for trial.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 28 and the Second Schedule of the Code of Criminal Procedure are controlled by other provisions of the Code, including Section 30, due to the opening clause 'subject to the other provisions of this Code'. A case pending before a Magistrate that ought to be tried by a Court of Session can be legally committed to the Court of Session under the power provided in Section 323 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: A person once convicted or acquitted cannot be tried for the same offense, as per Section 300(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which is based on the maxim ‘Nemo Debet Bis Vexari’; this principle is founded on the condition that the initial trial must be by a court of competent jurisdiction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that to ensure a fair trial for both the accused and the victim, and to avert a situation where the entire proceeding could be nullified for lack of jurisdiction, the case must be committed from the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate to the Court of Session. The Court determined that while the parties jointly requested this outcome, their suggested legal basis (Section 325, Cr.PC) was incorrect. The proper and legal exercise of power for this committal is under Section 323, Cr.PC.
legal_tests_applied: Competency of Jurisdiction for Double Jeopardy (Section 300(1) Cr.PC): The court reasoned that for the principle of 'Nemo Debet Bis Vexari' (no one should be vexed twice for the same cause) to apply, the initial trial must be conducted by a Court of competent jurisdiction. The risk that the current court lacked competence was a primary factor in the decision.

Right to Fair and Speedy Trial (Article 21): Citing Hussainara Khatoon and Nirmal Singh Kahlon, the court affirmed that a fair and speedy trial is a fundamental right for both the accused and the victim. Allowing the trial to continue in a court of questionable jurisdiction, which could lead to a fresh trial, would violate this right.

Statutory Power of Committal (Section 323 Cr.PC): The court identified Section 323, Cr.PC as the correct legal provision empowering a Magistrate to commit a case to the Court of Session at any stage before judgment if it appears the case is one which ought to be tried by that court.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument was only partially accepted; while the court agreed with the desired outcome of committing the case to the Court of Session, it rejected the suggested legal mechanism of exercising power under Section 325, Cr.PC, stating, 'We do not think it necessary to delve into that question as according to us this could be done legally in exercise of the power under Section 323, Cr. PC.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's core submission, made jointly with the appellant, that the case should be committed to a court of competent jurisdiction (the Court of Session) was accepted. The court agreed that this was necessary 'in order to have a fair trial, fair to both sides,' and to prevent a situation where the appellant might 'have to face fresh trial' if the original court was found to lack jurisdiction.
policy_considerations: To prevent a situation where a completed trial could be nullified, forcing a fresh trial: 'If ultimately, for any reason it is found that the trial was not before a Court of competent jurisdiction the appellant may again have to face fresh trial in view of the position obtained under Section 300(1), Cr.P.C.'

To uphold the fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21, especially given the 'disturbing fact' that the appellant had been an undertrial prisoner for over 8 years with the trial having made little progress.

To ensure a fair trial for both the accused and the victim, as established in Nirmal Singh Kahlon: 'In the said decision this Court held that both the accused and victim of a crime have right to fair trial and that fair investigation and fair trial are concomitant to preservation of the fundamental right of an accused under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.'
